newsitem.title: GERMANY: Karstadt stores lost money in 96 - magazine.
newsitem.headline: Karstadt stores lost money in 96 - magazine.

text.p: Germany's Karstadt AG lost 300 million marks last year at its department stores, but still expects to post a 100 million mark profit thanks to asset sales and profits at other units, Wirtschaftswoche said on Thursday.
The weekly news magazine said asset disposals would bring in extraordinary earnings of 300 million marks, and Karstadt would turn a profit at its travel agency and mail order units.

But, Wirtschaftswoche said, Karstadt's poor performance was leading to pressure from shareholders -- which include Deutsche Bank AG and Commerzbank AG -- on long-time chief executive Walter Deuss to quit.
The report, sourced to unnamed Karstadt shareholders, managers and labour representatives, said the shareholders wanted logistics director Klaus Eierhoff to replace Deuss.
Eierhoff wants to close 50 stores, while Deuss proposes shutting just 18 lossmaking outlets, Wirtschaftswoche said.
Karstadt and the two banks all declined to comment on the Wirtschaftswoche report.

The magazine also said that supervisory board head Guido Sandler wanted to call an urgent board meeting to discuss top personnel issues -- even though Deuss last autumn signed a new five-year contract.

Karstadt shares recovered strongly on the Frankfurt stock exchange after the Wirtschaftswoche report, gaining 15 to 545 marks. "That can only be because some traders see the obviously possible departure of chief executive Walter Deuss as positive for the company," one trader said.
Despite the bounce, Karstadt shares are still far below their 1995 peak of 678 marks.

The magazine warned that the possible departure of Deuss could lead to changes in accounting practices under a new chief executive which would reveal big hidden losses -- similar to those that rocked auto giant Daimler-Benz AG in 1995 after the departure of chief executive Edzard Reuter.

Karstadt has said it posted sales of 26.9 billion marks in 1996, down 0.3 percent on the previous year. The company said last November it would not be able to match its 1995 net profit of 109 million marks.
Deutsche and Commerzbank own 10 percent each in Karstadt, with a further 30 percent owned by the Hertie foundation representing the Karg family.
